messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Shopowner
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Vignette:
Sameer, a 29-year-old shopowner of South Asian descent, sought help after months of escalating distress following a period of physical abuse by a former romantic partner. The incident he recounted most vividly occurred late one evening in their shared apartment. An argument about his increasing independence, a topic that often ignited his partner’s volatile temper, had spiraled out of control. As the verbal assault intensified, so did the physical intimidation. He remembered the smell of his partner’s sweat, thick and cloying in the small space, just before the first shove, then the blows. He recalled the shock, the pain, and the overwhelming sense of helplessness, a feeling that still burned within him. He had come to believe, with a crushing certainty, that he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened, for not fighting back more effectively, for not protecting himself.

In the weeks and months that followed, Sameer found his world shrinking, his once-bustling shop becoming a source of constant anxiety. The smell of sweat or strong body odour from a customer leaning over the counter, or a delivery driver carrying heavy boxes, would instantly transport him back. Something in his surroundings could instantly bring back the full memory without warning, and a memory of the event would come to mind suddenly, vivid and disorienting. Sometimes, he would feel the intense rage that had been suppressed during the assault surge through him, a white-hot fury directed at his former partner, at himself, at the unfairness of it all. Other times, the emotional intensity of the event would wash over him without any clear image or memory, leaving him disoriented and terrified, his body reacting as if he were still in danger even when he knew intellectually he was safe behind his counter. He would feel his heart pound, his breath catch, a visceral response that convinced him his own body was an enemy he couldn't trust.

His days became a careful dance of avoidance. Certain conversation topics, particularly those touching on control, past relationships, or arguments, would send a cold dread through him, making him abruptly change the subject or retreat to the back room. As a shopowner, he was constantly interacting with the public, and this became increasingly difficult. Every time a stranger approached him, even for a simple transaction, he felt a profound sense of threat, his gaze darting, his muscles tensing, preparing for an attack that never came. He started delegating more tasks to his part-time employee, avoiding direct customer interactions where possible, and finding excuses to be in the stockroom. This shift in his approach to the business, once his pride, left him feeling increasingly isolated and incompetent, feeding into his deepening conviction that he couldn't rely on himself.

Evenings offered no respite. The thought of closing the shop, locking up, and walking home in the dimming light filled him with dread. He found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, the shadows outside his windows seeming to hold unseen dangers. This constant vigilance bled into his sleep, leaving him plagued by trouble falling or staying asleep. He would lie awake for hours, replaying snippets of the assault, his mind racing with "what ifs" and self-recriminations, his body too wired to rest. His current relationship, with a kind and supportive partner, was also suffering. He found himself withdrawing, unable to fully engage, haunted by the specter of his past.

The cumulative toll on his business and his personal life, along with the persistent, unshakeable feeling that he was fundamentally broken, finally prompted Sameer to seek help. He arrived at the clinic exhausted, his eyes shadowed, carrying the heavy burden of his guilt and his body’s relentless alarm system. What frightened him most was the idea that this might be his new normal, that he would forever be a prisoner to the past, unable to trust himself or the world around him. He desperately hoped for a way to quiet the constant internal alarms and regain some semblance of the person he used to be.
